The whole “20x” in Claude’s pricing is so misleading.

The $100 plan says 5x Pro limits, while the $200 plan says 20x Pro limits. That makes it sound like you’re getting 4x the usage.

But the 20x applies only to the 5-hour usage window. The weekly limit is basically just 2x the $100 plan.

I spent way too much time digging through the internet and Reddit to figure this out. They could’ve just stated the limits directly instead of marketing it as “20x.”

That alone would’ve saved me hours of confusion.

candidates.text:
Steal these:

We do influencer + UGC marketing for top AI companies, prediction markets, consumer brands, and B2B unicorns.

The playbook is simple: pay influencers or content creators to make content where your product is secondary or tertiary to the actual reason someone watches.

Some of our favorites:

B2B: Find someone who looks exactly like your target customer and make the content about the result.

“I own a med spa and we 10x’d our revenue doing cold outreach with .”

Consumer AI: Give the creator a real problem to solve in their daily life or work and have your product solve it.

Prediction markets: Build the product into an existing take. “Everyone thinks the Fed is cutting rates. Here’s where people are actually putting their money.”

Fintech: Put the product inside day-in-the-life, spending, investing, or “how I manage my money” content.

Cybersecurity: Recreate a scam, hack, or expensive mistake and make your product the thing that catches it.

Health: Build the product into a 30-day experiment around sleep, recovery, nutrition, or performance.

Beauty: Make the content about the transformation or routine. Your product just happens to be one of the things responsible for it.

The biggest mistake brands make is forcing the creator to talk about the product.

Instead, figure out what that creator’s audience already wants to watch, then find a natural way to make your product part of that content.

The more native the integration feels, the better it performs.

Sequoia partner Doug Leone reveals he got a root canal with no Novocaine to see if he was really a badass

"I had to get a root canal. And I had to go to a meeting right after that. I told the dentist, drill without any Novocaine.”

“My whole life, I wanted to see if I was a badass or not. Am I a fake badass that has this envelope nobody could tell, or am I really a badass on the inside?"

"He drilled and I jumped. And I told the dentist, I won't move again. And I didn't move again. I used the trick of thinking what it must be like to go to war and lose an arm or two legs. That's pain with consequences. Mine was pain with no consequences."

“It’s just nerve endings from there to my brain to my spine, f*ck it I’m not moving.”

"I had to go home and change my shirt because I was a puddle of sweat. But I didn't move. And so I love fear. It does wonders for me."

candidates.text:
🚨 ANDURIL CEO PLAYS POLITICS WITH INACCURATE DATA😒

The conniving part of Luckey’s H-1B argument is the statistical bait-and-switch.

He’s making a case about H-1B/high-skilled tech immigration, but then cites broad statistics about “immigrants” generally. That category can include family-sponsored immigrants, employment-based immigrants, refugees and asylees, diversity-visa immigrants, people who immigrated decades ago and are now citizens. Also depending on the dataset, either temporary or unauthorized immigrants.

So even if his figures about return migration and remittances are accurate for the population being studied, you cannot simply apply them to H-1B workers. Different populations, incomes, occupations, education levels, immigration pathways, and incentives to stay.

And high-skilled immigrants who leave the U.S. aren’t necessarily leaving because they happily decided to “take their savings home.” Visa constraints and employment-based green-card backlogs. Particularly for Indian and Chinese workers can make remaining in the U.S. extraordinarily difficult.

Meanwhile, the irony of using broad immigrant statistics to argue against high-skilled immigration is that Indian immigrants, who are heavily represented in the H-1B/high-skilled pipeline, are estimated to have one of the largest positive economic and fiscal impacts of any major immigrant-origin group. One recent analysis estimates that the average Indian immigrant reduces the national debt by more than $1.6 million over 30 years and increases GDP more than immigrants from any other country. (Manhattan Institute (https://t.co/Euv2bXMGqe)

And remittances aren’t the same thing as money simply “leaving the U.S. economy.” Immigrants spend most of their earnings domestically, pay taxes, and contribute to economic activity before sending money abroad.

If your argument is about H-1Bs, show H-1B data only. Don’t take statistics about immigrants as a whole, strip away the context behind why people leave, ignore the economic contribution of the highly skilled populations you’re actually discussing, and then present it as an argument against high-skilled immigration.

Would expect a better argument and not gaslighting from a man who has been a role model until now. Remember, this guy got $1 million from Peter Thiel at age 19 as a college dropout for an idea —> pure unfiltered nepotism and overselection.
